title: Seminar on the Future of Agriculture in Sri Lanka and Food Security
authors: Prof. Buddhi Marambe (Professor of Crop Science, University of Peradeniya), Dr. Parakkrama Waidyanatha (Former Chairman, Coconut Development Board), Prof. Jeevika Weerahewa (Professor of Agricultural Economics, University of Peradeniya), Mr. Rizvi Zaheed (Executive Director, Hayleys PLC), Dr. Nimal Sanderatne (Panel Chairman)
authorsLower: prof. buddhi marambe (professor of crop science, university of peradeniya), dr. parakkrama waidyanatha (former chairman, coconut development board), prof. jeevika weerahewa (professor of agricultural economics, university of peradeniya), mr. rizvi zaheed (executive director, hayleys plc), dr. nimal sanderatne (panel chairman)
abstract: Organized jointly by the Marga Institute and the Gamani Corea Foundation on January 30, 2017, this seminar examines the critical interplay between climate change, unpredictable agricultural policy, and long-term food security in Sri Lanka[cite: 3]. Key presentations highlight the challenges posed by rising global and domestic temperatures, severe droughts, and shifting monsoon patterns on rice yields[cite: 3]. The proceedings contrast historical reliance on rice imports with modern productivity milestones achieved through high-yielding crop varieties and scientific innovation[cite: 3]. Panelists critically evaluate recent domestic policy decisions—specifically unscientific bans on key agrochemicals—and underscore the urgent necessity for evidence-based policymaking[cite: 3]. Core strategic recommendations call for robust, 'no-regret' climate adaptation strategies, development of short-duration crop varieties, sustainable input management, and multi-stakeholder synergy across academia, government, and the private sector to safeguard national food security[cite: 3].

title: Policy Research on Agricultural Productivity
authors: Wasanthi Wickramasinghe (Team Leader), Parakrama Samaratunga, Aruppillai Thayaparan, Tilak Abeysinghe
authorsLower: wasanthi wickramasinghe (team leader), parakrama samaratunga, aruppillai thayaparan, tilak abeysinghe
abstract: This study conducts an in-depth policy research on Sri Lanka's agricultural productivity commissioned for the Agriculture Sector Modernization Project (ASMP). It evaluates total and partial factor productivity across ten import-substituting and export-promoting crop sectors from 1990 to 2018, decomposing agricultural output growth to assess the impacts of public investments in research, extension, irrigation, seeds, mechanization, credit, and crop insurance. Addressing institutional and regulatory constraints, private sector investment determinants, and trade policies, the report provides comprehensive recommendations and policy reform frameworks to enhance sector competitiveness, market responsiveness, and long-term resilience.

title: Post-war Accountability and Reconciliation: Creating an Inclusive Sri Lankan Identity
authors: Mr. Mangala Moonesinghe, Godfrey Gunatilleke, Mr. Asoka Gunawardena
authorsLower: mr. mangala moonesinghe, godfrey gunatilleke, mr. asoka gunawardena
abstract: This seminar report evaluates the Presidential Commission of Inquiry on Lessons Learnt and Reconciliation (LLRC) report as a vital instrument for post-war truth, accountability, and reconciliation in Sri Lanka[cite: 4, 5]. It examines the narrative of the final stages of the war, international and domestic responses, and the ongoing challenges regarding human rights, governance, and long-term harmonious co-existence[cite: 4, 5]. While recognizing the LLRC report's transparency, objective tone, and human-centric evidence gathering, the analysis highlights critical implementation gaps—notably the absence of an integrated, transparent institutional framework and action plan[cite: 4, 5]. The report stresses the necessity of aligning judicial, administrative, and political processes into a synchronized strategy to foster an inclusive national identity and sustainable peace[cite: 4, 5].

title: Is Rice Sector in Sri Lanka at Cross Roads?
authors: Jeevika Weerahewa, Department of Agricultural Economics and Business Management, Faculty of Agriculture, University of Peradeniya
authorsLower: jeevika weerahewa, department of agricultural economics and business management, faculty of agriculture, university of peradeniya
abstract: This study evaluates the structural trends, production dynamics, and trade vulnerabilities of Sri Lanka's rice sector, examining historical self-sufficiency patterns alongside the severe impact of the 2016/2017 drought on paddy cultivated extent[cite: 1]. Econometric estimations demonstrate that paddy production is significantly driven by irrigation access, seasonality, labor inputs, and specific fertilizer applications, with supply exhibiting greater responsiveness to output prices than input costs[cite: 1]. Despite historical market interventions—such as fertilizer subsidies, guaranteed prices, and import tariffs—the sector faces persistent contemporary challenges including malnutrition, low birth weight, micronutrient deficiencies, and international market volatility[cite: 1]. To navigate these issues, the analysis recommends transitioning toward climate-smart varietal development, water-saving technologies, market-targeted vouchers, secure land tenure, targeted safety-net buffer stocks, and evidence-based policy formulation[cite: 1].

title: Post-war Accountability and Reconciliation: Redefining Sri Lanka Identity
abstract: This seminar proceedings document evaluates the Lessons Learnt and Reconciliation Commission (LLRC) report as a vital mechanism for fostering post-war truth, accountability, and multi-ethnic reconciliation in Sri Lanka[cite: 7, 8]. The proceedings examine the commission's findings on military operations in the final stages of the conflict, while assessing domestic and international stakeholder responses[cite: 7, 8]. Highlighted by opening contexts and presentations from key speakers, the synthesis emphasizes that effective reconciliation requires integrating judicial, administrative, and socio-political frameworks into regular public administration rather than creating parallel systems[cite: 7, 8]. Key strategic recommendations include establishing an apex national steering body, maintaining transparency through dedicated public reporting, engaging civil society, and prioritizing victim-centric restitution alongside broader socio-economic development initiatives[cite: 7, 8].

title: Toxin-Free Nation' Agriculture Policy: Rhetoric & Repercussions
abstract: This presentation critically evaluates Sri Lanka's 'Toxin-Free Nation' (Vasa Visa Nethi Ratak) agricultural policy[cite: 1], analyzing the rhetoric and empirical repercussions of phasing out synthetic fertilizers and chemical pesticides in favor of traditional rice varieties and organic alternatives[cite: 1]. The analysis refutes claims linking glyphosate and agrochemicals to Chronic Kidney Disease of unknown etiology (CKDu), citing international scientific consensus and WHO/FAO findings[cite: 1]. Historical data shows that modern high-yielding rice varieties dramatically increased productivity[cite: 1], whereas forcing a return to low-yielding traditional varieties across 30% of farmland severely threatens national food security and rice supply[cite: 1]. The paper highlights that alternative bio-fertilizers and organic inputs cannot fully compensate for nitrogen deficits at scale[cite: 1]. Consequently, the author recommends evidence-based decision-making, consultation with mainstream agricultural scientists, and balanced media coverage rather than reliance on unverified organic policy rhetoric[cite: 1].

title: Future of Agriculture and Food Security in Sri Lanka
authors: Prof. Buddhi Marambe, Dr. Parakrama Waidyanatha, Prof. Jeevika Weerahewa, Mr. Rizvi Zaheed, Dr. Nimal Sanderatne
authorsLower: prof. buddhi marambe, dr. parakrama waidyanatha, prof. jeevika weerahewa, mr. rizvi zaheed, dr. nimal sanderatne
abstract: This summary report covers a seminar held on January 30, 2017, at the Bandaranaike Memorial International Conference Hall (BMICH), organized by the Marga Institute and the Gamani Corea Foundation on the future of Sri Lankan agriculture and food security. Key discussions highlighted the challenges posed by global climate change, rapid global population growth, strict land and water constraints, and rising temperatures affecting rice production and agricultural stability. Presenters and experts evaluated historical agricultural shifts, high-yielding crop varieties, technology integration, chemical inputs, and climate adaptation strategies required to maintain long-term food security.

title: Post-war accountability and reconciliation: Redefining Sri Lanka Identity
abstract: This report synthesizes the proceedings of a seminar organized by the Marga Institute to evaluate the Lessons Learnt and Reconciliation Commission (LLRC) report as a tool for truth, accountability, and post-war reconciliation in Sri Lanka. The seminar examined the narrative of final military operations, human rights violations, and civilian casualty estimates, concluding that while civilian targeting was not government policy, specific abuses require further domestic judicial and administrative investigation. It reviews international and domestic stakeholder reactions—ranging from criticism by INGOs to support from key international actors—and proposes a multi-pronged implementation strategy combining judicial, administrative, and political-social measures to foster a unified Sri Lankan identity.

title: Establishing an Accountability Process in Sri Lanka: Realizing Truth, Justice and Reparation
authors: Dr. Godfrey Gunatilleke, Dr. Dayan Jayatilleke, Prof. Rajiva Wijesinghe, Ms. Tamara Kunanayagam, Dr. Jehan Perera, Gehan Gunatilleke
authorsLower: dr. godfrey gunatilleke, dr. dayan jayatilleke, prof. rajiva wijesinghe, ms. tamara kunanayagam, dr. jehan perera, gehan gunatilleke
abstract: This document highlights key presentations and discussions from a seminar convened by the Marga Institute on Sri Lanka's post-conflict accountability framework. The proceedings evaluate the friction between the international narrative represented by the UN Secretary General's Panel of Experts (POE) report and the domestic findings of the Lessons Learnt and Reconciliation Commission (LLRC). Presenters examine geopolitical dynamics, international diplomatic pressures surrounding UNHRC resolutions, and domestic challenges to establishing a credible truth-seeking process. Strategic recommendations emphasize transitioning toward a consensus-based restorative justice framework, addressing domestic institutional gaps, engaging multi-party consultations including the TNA, and formulating an independent national foreign policy grounded in domestic social justice.

title: Post-war Accountability and Reconciliation: Creating an Inclusive Sri Lankan Identity
abstract: This report synthesizes the proceedings and outcomes of a civil society seminar organized by the Marga Institute on February 9, 2012, to evaluate the Presidential Commission of Inquiry on Lessons Learnt and Reconciliation (LLRC) Report in Sri Lanka. The seminar examined the LLRC's findings across three main dimensions: post-war accountability and international humanitarian law (IHL) during the final stages of the conflict, the state of human rights and governance, and long-term reconciliation mechanisms. While acknowledging limitations in the LLRC's scope regarding victim-centered truth-telling, discussants highlighted positive contributions, including the rejection of the zero-casualty claim, documentation of disappearances, and recommendations for restorative justice. The report outlines domestic and international stakeholder responses and presents Marga Institute's strategic proposals for an integrated, multi-tiered institutional framework to mainstream LLRC recommendations into regular administrative systems, foster democratic governance, and support an inclusive Sri Lankan identity.

title: Issues of Truth and Accountability Narrative III: The Last Stages of the War in Sri Lanka
authors: Godfrey Gunatilleke, Jeevan Thiagarajah, Asoka Gunawardene
authorsLower: godfrey gunatilleke, jeevan thiagarajah, asoka gunawardene
partnerName: Marga Institute & Consortium of Humanitarian Agencies (CHA)
abstract: This report presents an alternate narrative—termed the 'Third Narrative'—concerning the last stages of the Sri Lankan civil war (2006–2009), produced in response to the March 2014 UNHRC resolution. It provides a critical evaluation of existing contradictory accounts, particularly contrasting the United Nations Secretary-General's Panel of Experts (PoE) report with the Sri Lankan Government's Lessons Learnt and Reconciliation Commission (LLRC) report. The document analyzes the methodology and evidentiary bases of these reports, highlighting key gaps, flawed analytical approaches regarding International Humanitarian Law (IHL), and issues related to distinction and proportionality. It details the tactical progression of the war, the LTTE's strategy of utilizing trapped civilians as human shields and firing from No-Fire Zones, as well as the Sri Lankan military's operational responses. Furthermore, it assesses the multi-tiered accountabilities of the LTTE, the Sri Lankan Government and armed forces, the international community, and the United Nations agencies, proposing a balanced, impartial evaluation to foster genuine domestic reconciliation and transitional justice.

title: Examination of the Current Education System of Sri Lanka in Relation to the Provision of Prerequisites and Attributes Concerning Very High Human Development
authors: Dr. Godfrey Gunatilleke, Prof. Tilak Abeysinghe
authorsLower: dr. godfrey gunatilleke, prof. tilak abeysinghe
abstract: This report examines the current education system of Sri Lanka to assess its alignment with prerequisites and attributes necessary to achieve Very High Human Development (VHHD) status. Highlighting positive achievements such as high secondary school enrolment rates, gender parity in schooling, and competitive mean years of schooling comparable to benchmarks like Finland, Singapore, and South Korea, the report contrasts these achievements with key structural deficiencies. Major issues identified include extreme school system diversity and inequality, underfunded infrastructure in smaller provincial schools, an over-concentration of students in less employable Arts streams, low participation in tertiary and STEM education, and brain drain among tertiary-educated professionals. To bridge these gaps, the study provides strategic recommendations focusing on expanding English-medium instruction, upgrading vocational education programs (NVQ), rebalancing university streams toward high-demand sectors, and reforming institutional structures to support economic growth and human development goals.

title: The Impact of COVID-19 on Early Childhood Development Services in Sri Lanka
abstract: This study assesses the severe disruptions to Early Childhood Development (ECD) services in Sri Lanka caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and prolonged lockdowns starting in March 2020. Based on an August 2021 telephone survey conducted by the World Bank and Marga Institute across 15 districts, the study synthesizes data from 300 primary caregivers, 100 ECD teachers, and 10 ECD officers across urban, rural, and estate sectors. Key findings highlight negative health and behavioral impacts on children—including missed clinic appointments (22%), food insecurity, irritability, and behavioral shifts—alongside major drops in teacher income, job losses, and center closures. Alternate home-based and online learning strategies were deployed, though limited by persistent digital infrastructure gaps and lack of teacher training. The paper underscores urgent policy and practice implications, emphasizing the need for targeted nutritional interventions, enhanced digital educational infrastructure, and structured support for ECD personnel to mitigate long-term development setbacks.

title: Dream of a Workforce to Meet Future Labor Market Demands
abstract: This assessment by Dr. Harsha Aturupane examines Sri Lanka's education and training system in the context of economic growth and shifting labor market demands[cite: 1]. While Sri Lanka maintains high primary and secondary school enrollment rates with gender parity[cite: 1], learning achievements decline markedly at higher secondary levels alongside substantial disparities across school types[cite: 1]. Local enterprises report skill shortages as a major operational constraint, surpassing levels observed in peer middle-income countries[cite: 1]. The analysis identifies significant bottlenecks in teacher management, quality assurance, and the Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) sector, particularly minimal employer involvement, slow NVQ framework implementation, and qualified instructor shortages[cite: 1]. To accelerate economic transformation, the report emphasizes system alignment, policy reform, enhanced incentive structures, and targeted higher education improvements to better bridge human capital with future industry needs[cite: 1].

title: Higher Education - The Continuing Crisis
abstract: This analysis by the Marga Institute examines the ongoing crisis in Sri Lankan higher education, specifically focusing on the prolonged confrontation between the government and the Federation of University Teachers' Associations (FUTA). The report evaluates the two primary bones of contention: FUTA's demand for basic salary increases based on the Jiffry-Malik Ranasinghe Committee recommendations, and the allocation of 6% of GDP to education. The paper highlights the lack of transparency regarding existing allowances (such as research and development top-ups) versus basic salary structures, alongside government concerns regarding macro-economic stability and spillover wage demand effects across the wider public service sector. Additionally, it addresses the irrelevance of international wage comparisons in domestic salary policy. The institute proposes a speedy resolution through a National Salaries and Wages Policy framework, advocating for a National Commission to consolidate allowances into a structured national wage hierarchy prioritizing university academics.

title: Female Labour Force Participation-Impact on the Household in Sri Lanka’s Transition to Very High Human Development (VHHD) Status
abstract: This study examines the paradox of low female labour force participation (FLFP) in Sri Lanka despite key preconditions such as high female education attainments, low fertility rates, and small household sizes. Drawing on a sub-sample of nearly 5,000 young functional families from the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES 2012/2013), the research compares the socioeconomic, demographic, and capability profiles of working females (WFs) and non-working females (NWFs). Using statistical evaluations including Mann-Whitney U tests and a composite Capability Index, the analysis demonstrates that WFs generally possess higher capability scores and smaller household burdens, whereas NWFs prioritize domestic care responsibilities due to lack of enabling institutional environments. The study highlights policy gaps in combining work and domestic care, recommending target interventions such as expanded tertiary education, skill upgrading for secondary-educated women, institutional support for home-based work, and flexible working arrangements to enhance both household well-being and national economic productivity.

title: Female Labour Force Participation-Impact on the Household in Sri Lanka’s Transition to Very High Human Development (VHHD) Status
abstract: This study addresses the Sri Lankan conundrum of low female labour force participation (FLFP) despite favourable preconditions such as high female literacy, low fertility rates, and small household sizes. Utilizing data from a subset of nearly 5,000 young functional families in the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES 2012/2013), the research compares working females (WFs) and non-working females (NWFs) using descriptive indicators, Mann-Whitney U non-parametric statistical tests, and a composite Capability Index. Findings reveal that while WFs generally possess higher overall capability indices and smaller family burdens, many NWFs refrain from joining the workforce due to household care priorities and the lack of institutional care alternatives. The report emphasizes key policy measures to facilitate FLFP, including expanded tertiary education, skill upgrading for secondary-educated women, institutional support for home-based work, flexible employment models, and care network infrastructures.

title: MCC Land Project in Sri Lanka
abstract: This presentation outlines the MCC Land Project in Sri Lanka, based on a 2016 constraints-to-growth analysis that identified difficult access to land for investment purposes as a primary economic bottleneck. The project proposes interventions across 7 districts along the Colombo-Trincomalee Economic Corridor, focusing on inventorying state land, modernizing the deeds registry, improving valuation systems, converting deeds to title registration, and establishing a land policy body.

title: The 5 Point Plan and the 10 Point Agreement
abstract: This paper critically examines the UNF's 5 Point Plan and the 10 Point Agreement signed between the UNF and a section of the SLFP following the Sri Lankan parliamentary elections in 2015. It highlights the disconnect between political rhetoric, wish-list manifestos, and basic economic principles such as opportunity costs and resource constraints. Drawing upon Shelton Wanasinghe's 1987 Administrative Reforms Report, the author stresses that fragmented, ad-hoc policy implementation leads to chaotic outcomes. The document outlines a comprehensive framework for development management, detailing seven core pillars—ranging from savings/investment and macroeconomics to infrastructure, education, and health—and emphasizes the foundational role of governance institutions and public service leadership.

title: MCC Transport Project: Connecting People and Goods to Employment and Markets in Sri Lanka
partnerName: Millennium Challenge Corporation / Government of Sri Lanka (GoSL)
abstract: This presentation outlines the MCC Transport Project aimed at addressing core transport constraints in Sri Lanka, specifically traffic congestion in the Western Province and slow inter-regional movement of goods and people. Key drivers of these issues include rising population growth, rapid urbanization, private transport reliance, and sub-optimal public transit provision. Proposed interventions include Advanced Traffic Management Systems (ATMS) across eight major corridors in the Colombo Metropolitan Region, comprehensive bus modernization (including automated fare collection, GPS tracking, and safety measures), and Central Ring Road network improvements in the provinces.

title: Presentation on MCC Compact: $480 Million Grant - Increasing Growth through Improved Transportation Infrastructure and Land Administration
authors: Millennium Challenge Corporation, Government of Sri Lanka
authorsLower: millennium challenge corporation, government of sri lanka
abstract: This presentation outlines the $480 Million (86.4 Billion LKR) grant agreement between the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) and the Government of Sri Lanka (GoSL). Based on a constraint analysis conducted with Harvard University identifying weak transport infrastructure and land administration as key binding constraints to economic growth, the compact allocates $350 Million for transport modernization (Advanced Traffic Management System, Bus Transport Modernization, and Upgrading Provincial Roads) and $67 Million for land administration reform (state land inventory, digitizing records, scaling Bim Saviya, and valuation support). The report details project costs, projected economic rates of return, key benefits, and oversight mechanisms, while addressing public misconceptions regarding military involvement, land ownership, and regional development corridors.

title: SUSTAINABILITY THROUGH ENGAGEMENT TO MANAGE URBANIZATION IN SRI LANKA
abstract: This presentation addresses the challenges of urbanization in Sri Lanka and explores sustainable management frameworks through active engagement. It examines the divergence between urban policies and practical programs, analyzes whether the growth of Tier 2 cities represents an emerging opportunity or a push-out effect, and advocates for a global learning, local solutions paradigm shift. The document introduces a comparative framework utilizing global case studies, including Tax Increment Financing in Johannesburg, the Urban Upgrading Project in Ho Chi Minh City, and housing and social sustainability initiatives in Quezon City.

title: The Numbers Game: Politics of Retributive Justice
authors: Independent Diaspora Analysis Group - Sri Lanka
authorsLower: independent diaspora analysis group - sri lanka
partnerName: Independent Diaspora Analysis Group - Sri Lanka (IDAG-S)
abstract: This discussion paper examines the accuracy of civilian fatality estimates from the final stages of Eelam War IV in Sri Lanka, specifically scrutinizing numbers such as 40,000, 70,000, and 147,000. Utilizing a semi-empirical methodology, the study analyzes numerical data, satellite imagery, eyewitness testimony, and population statistics. The report argues that the widely cited figure of 330,000 people trapped in the No-Fire-Zone in February 2009 is an over-inflation derived from unreliable methods, thereby undermining the calculations for mass civilian deaths. By establishing a casualty enumeration methodology based on injury-to-death ratios, the analysis suggests a more probable range of 15,000 to 18,000 truly civilian fatalities. The study concludes that international bodies and human rights organizations have subjectively interpreted legal definitions and ignored complex ground realities—such as the LTTE's aggressive conscription, use of human shields, and blending of combatants with civilians—to advance a pre-defined political agenda aimed at international intervention and regime change.

title: VISTAS OF PROSPERITY - ENVIRONMENT ANALYSIS AND WAY FORWARD
abstract: This document provides an environmental analysis and way forward based on the 'Vistas of Prosperity' framework. It highlights key observations regarding climate change, energy targets, agricultural policies, and environmental regulation. The analysis identifies a target of 80% renewable energy by 2030, contrasting it with the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) Generation Plan's 35% target and noting a lack of clear action plans and institutional skill gaps. It also addresses issues related to fertilizer policies, pollution, biodiversity conservation through a proposed centralized authority, and the critical systemic gaps in capacity and capability at the institutional level that threaten the environment.

title: Technology-based society elements in National Policy Framework Vistas of Prosperity & Splendour
abstract: This presentation analyzes the digital technology-based actions and initiatives proposed within Sri Lanka's National Policy Framework, 'Vistas of Prosperity & Splendour'. Employing filters of coherence and implementability, it critiques proposed actions across key areas, including software export promotion, digital inclusivity, citizen-centric digital government, judicial efficiency, and innovation hubs. The review highlights specific execution challenges, such as the viability of rural IT centers, the practical scaling of 14,000+ local service centers, and the necessity of stable, industry-backed frameworks like the National Export Strategy (2018-2022). It advocates for comprehensive online integrations, stable funding for research institutions, and the urgent finalization of data protection and cyber security legislation to truly transition Sri Lanka into an efficient, technology-based society.

title: The capacity building required for policy implementation
partnerName: National Policy Framework Vistas of Prosperity and Splendour
abstract: This presentation outlines the capacity building required for effective public policy implementation within the framework of 'Vistas of Prosperity and Splendour.' Defining public policy as government choices of action or inaction, it details 10 key national policies spanning national security, economic development, and technology. Successful implementation relies on three main pillars: enhancing the knowledge, skills, and attitudes of the public sector; leveraging private sector public-private partnerships; and fostering active community participation. Key structural strategies include merit-based appointments for ministry secretaries and state institution heads, systematic career development and training, the removal of redundant regulations, and establishing an efficient governance mechanism that incorporates community and professional feedback.

title: Health accountability in the industrial sector
abstract: Examines workplace health regulations, industrial waste control, and occupational safety measures within Sri Lanka's growing urban manufacturing sectors. It assesses corporate and public enforcement gaps and recommends updating industrial monitoring laws.

title: Health and nutrition development in rural communities
abstract: An empirical analysis tracking the long-term impact of community-managed food programs on maternal and child health indicators. The study emphasizes the role of localized health groups in improving nutritional outcomes without relying heavily on central state funding.

title: Health & development in sri lanka
abstract: A baseline case study illustrating Sri Lanka's historical achievement of strong health indices despite a low per capita GDP. It examines the synergy between early welfare choices, universal schooling access, and free primary care distribution models.

title: Health in development
abstract: A policy paper examining the impacts of macro-structural adjustment loans on state health budgets in South Asia. The paper argues for protective mechanisms to insulate primary care and preventative health budgets from macro-economic adjustments.

title: Health policy in sri lanka
authors: Ministry of Health, Marga Consultation Panel
authorsLower: ministry of health, marga consultation panel
abstract: A review document summarizing institutional choices, hospital infrastructure expansions, and systemic human resource challenges facing Sri Lanka's dual public-private healthcare system at the start of the 1990s.

title: Health research with reference to intersectoral action
abstract: Addresses the methodological changes required to transition from purely clinical health studies toward cross-cutting, intersectoral research frameworks that analyze socio-economic and environmental factors.

title: Intersectoral action for health - sri lanka study
abstract: A comprehensive national study compiled for the Technical Discussions at the 39th World Health Assembly. It serves as a key reference on how Sri Lanka coordinated water, housing, food subsidies, and clinical healthcare to improve demographic metrics.

title: Inter-city workshop on primary health care in urban areas
abstract: Proceedings from a multi-city municipal workshop focusing on sanitary challenges, clean water access, and infectious disease containment across expanding low-income urban settlements in Colombo and regional capitals.

title: Intersectoral action for health 1981
abstract: An early policy layout detailing structural plans to link primary healthcare expansion with agricultural irrigation strategies and food distribution channels during the implementation of the Accelerated Mahaweli Development Program.

title: Intersectoral action for health at district level
abstract: An operational assessment examining how District Development Councils and local secretariats coordinate health programs, focusing on administrative bottlenecks and resource constraints in rural areas.

title: Action research project on health nutrition home gardens
abstract: A micro-level operational report summarizing an action-research intervention aimed at reducing nutritional deficiencies in rural Sri Lankan households. The study documents how structured home garden setups enhance dietary diversification, bolster food security, and act as scalable localized additions to national primary care networks.

title: An indicative framework for the shd profile for sri lanka
abstract: Establishes a quantitative diagnostic schema for measuring Sustainable Human Development (SHD) across Sri Lanka's key districts. The report frames baseline indices covering chronic poverty vectors, basic sanitation access, and systemic social protections to steer structural national allocation planning.

title: Burden of disease and equity
abstract: This research analyzes health disparities by mapping out the epidemiological transition toward chronic non-communicable diseases in Sri Lanka. It assesses how treatment-related expenses burden lower-income tiers and recommends shifting resource allocations toward protective, cross-cutting equity measures.

title: Children in sri lanka
abstract: A macro-demographic assessment exploring child welfare indicators, focusing on infant survival rates, educational access, and regional malnutrition. The paper outlines strategic policy recommendations designed to address regional disparities, particularly within remote plantation zones and underdeveloped rural sectors.

title: Community health workers
abstract: Evaluates the training protocols, functional limitations, and systemic integration of community-level health workers within Sri Lanka's healthcare system. It highlights their role in narrowing the service gap between formalized regional clinics and isolated rural populations.

title: Development of primary health care in country paper
authors: Ministry of Health Sri Lanka, Marga Institute
authorsLower: ministry of health sri lanka, marga institute
abstract: A country-level synthesis tracing the integration of the Alma-Ata Declaration goals into Sri Lanka's national health strategy. It documents the evolution of decentralized health units, preventative infrastructure networks, and local health volunteer engagement models.

title: Enhancement of social security for the poor
abstract: Investigates the structural shifts from early post-independence universal welfare schemes to targeted assistance programs. The analysis outlines policy pathways to enhance safety nets, minimize administrative leakage, and protect lower-income groups during economic transitions.

title: Evaluation of the unicef programme in the estate sector
abstract: An field evaluation examining UNICEF-funded healthcare, water supply, and sanitation interventions across Sri Lanka's tea plantation sectors. It highlights structural issues in project execution, localized health outcomes, and challenges in sustaining long-term infrastructure.

title: Examples of health policy analysis
abstract: A methodological manual illustrating policy evaluation models for developing country frameworks. It provides case studies across budget distributions, legislative health measures, and multi-agency coordination to guide health planning teams.

title: Gampaha health project
abstract: A detailed profile of a localized pilot project in the Gampaha district designed to improve intersectoral coordination. The paper analyzes collaboration models between agricultural extensions, education offices, and sanitary engineers to address localized health challenges.

title: Guidelines for policies and programmes on intersectoral action for health
abstract: An operational guidebook outlining steps to integrate health targets into broader national development plans. It includes frameworks for institutionalizing inter-ministerial task forces, sharing data across sectors, and creating joint resource pools.

title: Accountability for health
abstract: This background study conceptualizes administrative, operational, and civic accountability in public health infrastructure. Prepared for the global Intersectoral Action for Health initiatives, it evaluates structural linkages where non-health ministries directly affect macro-health dynamics, advocating for systemic monitoring and binding state impact audits.

title: Female Labour Force Participation-Impact on the Household in Sri Lanka’s Transition to Very High Human Development (VHHD) Status
abstract: This study examines the paradox of low female labour force participation (FLFP) in Sri Lanka despite key preconditions such as high female education attainments, low fertility rates, and small household sizes. Drawing on a sub-sample of nearly 5,000 young functional families from the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES 2012/2013), the research compares the socioeconomic, demographic, and capability profiles of working females (WFs) and non-working females (NWFs). Using statistical evaluations including Mann-Whitney U tests and a composite Capability Index, the analysis demonstrates that WFs generally possess higher capability scores and smaller household burdens, whereas NWFs prioritize domestic care responsibilities due to lack of enabling institutional environments. The study highlights policy gaps in combining work and domestic care, recommending target interventions such as expanded tertiary education, skill upgrading for secondary-educated women, institutional support for home-based work, and flexible working arrangements to enhance both household well-being and national economic productivity.

title: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) Strategy for Colombo Trincomalee Economic Corridor (CTEC) - Strategic Plan for CTEC with additions March 2019
partnerName: Ministry of Youth and Skills Development & Asian Development Bank (ADB)
abstract: This document outlines a comprehensive Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) strategy designed for the Colombo Trincomalee Economic Corridor (CTEC) for the period 2022-2032. Managed by the Ministry of Skills Development and guided by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) demand forecasts across ten districts, the strategy seeks to prepare a technical workforce for over 1.2 million new jobs in growth industries including Apparel, Food Processing, Electrical Equipment, and Pharmaceuticals. The Marga approach identifies institutional challenges such as high trainee dropout rates, a lack of awareness of the National Vocational Qualification (NVQ) framework, and low wage structures for trainers. To match labor supply with demand, the document recommends establishing specialized Sector Skills Councils, launching integrated Labour Market Information Systems (LMIS) via platforms like youthjobs.lk, implementing Competency-Based Training (CBET), and establishing Centres of Excellence in Kalutara, Gampaha, and Trincomalee.

title: Development Dialogues: Issues and Challenges (Final Report)
partnerName: The Asia Foundation & Local CSO Partners
abstract: This final report outlines a community-driven initiative across six selected villages in Trincomalee, Mannar, and Kalutara districts in Sri Lanka. Working in close collaboration with active civil society organizations and supported by the Asia Foundation, the research employed multi-stage workshops ('Development Dialogues') and household visits to map local aspirations and development priorities. The findings document severe economic challenges, including water shortages, land ownership disputes, high unemployment, and poverty, alongside social barriers such as drug addiction and prevailing caste-based conflicts. The study details community-suggested solutions, including skills development, vocational training, agricultural infrastructure (agri-wells), and counseling. It highlights systemic hurdles like the absence of a proper marketing mechanism for local industries and insufficient government financial allocations, advocating for enhanced public-citizen collaboration and robust local monitoring mechanisms.

title: Community Perceptions on Governance, Cohesion, and Economic Shocks: Initial Survey under Development Dialogues
partnerName: The Asia Foundation & Local CSO Partners
abstract: This study presents the findings of an initial survey of 199 respondents across Mannar, Trincomalee, and Kalutara districts, evaluating community-level decision-making, intergroup cohesion, and the domestic impacts of the economic crisis. The survey reveals that 56% of respondents overall feel excluded from government decision-making, with significant regional variations (71% participation in Mannar versus 10% in Kalutara). Over 88% of respondents reported being deeply affected by the current cost-of-living crisis and economic shocks. To cope, households in Trincomalee and Kalutara increased income through cultivation and livestock farming, while those in Mannar utilized saved money sparingly. The study also measures high community cohesion and cooperation in Kalutara but identifies crucial policy gaps in gender equality and the recognition of rights for vulnerable groups.

title: The Impact of COVID-19 on Early Childhood Development (ECD) Services in Sri Lanka: Findings from a Telephone Survey
partnerName: National Secretariat of Early Childhood Development
abstract: This report details the findings of a telephone survey conducted in August 2021 to understand how the COVID-19 pandemic and prolonged school closures affected child development outcomes and early childhood development (ECD) services in Sri Lanka. Gathering data from 300 caregivers, 100 ECD teachers, and 10 ECD officers across 15 districts, the study evaluates pandemic coping mechanisms. Results demonstrate a strong level of home-based caregiver engagement, with 95% of caregivers actively playing, singing, or reading to their children. To bridge remote education gaps, 80% of ECD teachers actively provided workbooks and home-based instructions to caregivers, and 47% (rising to 77% in the estate sector) conducted physical home visits. The findings provide critical insights to inform the resilience and strengthening of ECD services during and after public health shocks.

title: Women’s Role in Peacebuilding and Inter-Community Harmony: Community Assessments and Surveys
abstract: This presentation summarizes findings from community assessments and online surveys examining communal harmony and trust across multiple Sri Lankan districts. The research shows that 95% of respondents believe women's involvement in communal harmony programs exerts a far-reaching influence on peacebuilding. However, significant vulnerabilities remain, with 23% of female respondents expressing a lack of faith that Sri Lankan society can live in peace and harmony, and 20% lacking trust specifically in Sinhalese-community relations. The study highlights religious tensions as primary drivers of regional conflict and emphasizes the necessity of proactive peacebuilding, educating youth on civil obligations, and utilizing cross-ethnic socio-economic institutions (such as farmer organizations and development societies) to support sustainable social cohesion.

title: Disinformation and Hate Speech: Impact on Minority Communities in Sri Lanka
abstract: Conducted from September to October 2022, this study combines media monitoring and local field assessments to evaluate the impact of online and offline hate speech and disinformation on Sri Lankan minorities. Based on a quantitative survey of 300 minority group members and 150 in-depth qualitative interviews of both minority and majority Sinhalese respondents, the study maps ethnic hotspots. Key findings demonstrate that minorities frequently encounter offensive ethnic comments (primarily in Kalutara, Gampaha, Colombo, and Vavuniya districts) and encounter stereotyping regarding food, dress, and physical appearance. The research classifies community leaders into three categories based on their reaction to hate speech, outlining a strategic way forward to combat anti-social media content and promote national unity.

title: Developing Case Studies: Social and Economic Benefits of Seed Grants (INSPIRED Project)
abstract: This extensive report presents detailed case studies of sole and joint entrepreneurs in Ampara, Batticaloa, and Trincomalee who received seed grants under the INSPIRED project. Working through local organizations like GAFSO, ESCO, and Sarvodaya, the initiative provided training in finance, bookkeeping, marketing, and digital tools. Grantees utilized seed funding to purchase essential machinery (such as Juki sewing machines and packaging tools), increasing business productivity and fostering female financial independence. Critically, the project utilized mandatory multi-ethnic business networks and exhibitions, which successfully dismantled negative cultural stereotypes and fostered trust among Sinhalese, Tamil, and Muslim participants, demonstrating that economic development and social reconciliation are mutually reinforcing.

title: Survey to Ascertain the Capacity of Public Institutions to Implement the National Language Policy (NLEAP Survey Report)
partnerName: National Languages Equality Advancement Project (NLEAP) & Official Languages Commission (OLC)
abstract: This comprehensive survey assesses the capacity of 33 public institutions in Sri Lanka to comply with the Official Languages Policy (OLP), requiring services in Sinhala, Tamil, and English. Combining 'Mystery Customer' audits, visitors' surveys (500 sample), and small group discussions, the study evaluates signage, application forms, phone assistance, and bilingual reception. The results highlight severe compliance gaps: only 53% of institutions featured Tamil-speaking receptionists, and only 47% had Tamil application forms available. Furthermore, 25% of Tamil-speaking visitors encountered language-based service issues, rising to 85% in Nuwara Eliya. The report recommends systemic reforms, including simplifying form terminology, hiring dedicated language and trilingual officers, conducting cultural Change Management, and adopting e-governance solutions.

title: Evaluation of the Self Employment Promotion Initiative (SEPI) Loan Scheme
partnerName: Ministry of Skills Development and Vocational Training (MSDVT)
abstract: This report evaluates the effectiveness of the SEPI loan scheme among 500 randomly selected vocational graduates from the VTA, NAITA, DTET, and NYSC. It assesses how trainees utilized financial aid to start or expand businesses. The profile shows a high proportion of female loan recipients (57%), with 36% of all trainees specializing in Beauty Culture (representing 70% of females). While general satisfaction with vocational training was high (95%), the lack of start-up capital and procedural bank delays emerge as major business obstacles. The study recommends diversifying training into agro-industry and food preservation, improving coordination with regional banks, providing tracer-monitoring support, and issuing printed introduction leaflets to streamline loan access.

title: Demographics and Professional Characteristics of Justice Sector Actors: Court Users, Lawyers, and Police Officers
abstract: This quantitative research compilation profiles the demographic characteristics and operational interactions of key actors in the Sri Lankan justice sector, including court users, lawyers, and police officers. Tracking interactions across a 100-user court sample, the data indicates an average of 12 visits per court business, noting that language barriers and complex forms present key obstacles. It details a 100-lawyer sample (58% male, 42% female, averaging 11 years in profession) and a 100-police officer sample (98% male, 2% female), mapping their professional backgrounds, specialization areas, and service experience to provide an empirical basis for systemic justice sector reforms.

title: Mapping of Data Collection, Analysis and Dissemination Capacity of Key Justice Sector Institutions in Sri Lanka
partnerName: Ministry of Justice & Justice Reform Programme (JURE)
abstract: This mapping study audits the data collection, analysis, and dissemination capacities of core justice sector institutions in Sri Lanka to track progress against Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 16 indicators. It reviews reporting protocols across agencies including the Sri Lanka Police, Department of Prisons, and Ministry of Justice, noting that only 10 to 12 indicators are active. The study identifies key challenges, such as fragmented and manual data entry systems and severe staff shortages. It outlines immediate short-term recommendations (drafting clear reporting guidelines, basic staff training), mid-term goals (establishing dedicated data entry teams, regular audits), and a long-term target of building a unified, comprehensive digital case management system.

title: Compliance with the Official Languages Policy (OLP) at Public Institutions: 2023 Update
abstract: Presented on March 21, 2023, this update evaluates compliance levels with the Official Languages Policy (OLP) at select local government authorities, hospitals, and police stations across multiple provinces. Utilizing mystery customer audits, supply checklists, and visitor surveys, the study monitors visual signs, trilingual documentation, receptionist assistance, and telephone support. While signboards and the availability of female receptionists to assist women customers show high compliance, telephone and written assistance in minority languages remain weak. Notable improvements are documented in Vavuniya and the Eastern Province compared to 2021, and the report recommends local geography-based cadre allocations, trilingual increments, and specialized attitude-change workshops for public officials.

title: Survey on Compliance with the Official Languages Policy (OLP) - 2014 Report
partnerName: Foreign Affairs Trade and Development Canada (DFATD) & National Languages Project
abstract: This report presents the findings of the 2014 OLP compliance survey across 50 target institutions, comparing the results directly with the 2007/08 baseline. It evaluates the 'supply' capacity of public bodies and the 'demand' experience of citizens. The data reveals that while bilingual human resources have grown, substantial public-facing deficits persist: half of the institutions lack bilingual receptionists, and over half cannot process incoming bilingual phone calls. On the demand side, 27% of citizens report language as a major barrier to services, and 33.4% of Tamil speakers face issues filling out complex forms. The report recommends formalized public administration incentive systems, trilingual recruitments, and creating community-level language aid clinics.

title: Public Institutions and Service Delivery: Re-defining the Role of Public Institutions
abstract: This policy monograph explores the re-definition of public institutions' roles and structural capacities in Sri Lanka. It aligns public administration reforms with ten national priorities, including national security, anti-corruption, technology-based society, and environmental sustainability. The author emphasizes that institutional service delivery must be restructured around modern public management principles to support the overarching national policy goals of creating a productive citizen, a happy family, a disciplined society, and a prosperous nation. It advocates for tech-enabled administrative tools, streamlined procedures, and citizen-centric performance monitoring.

title: Survey on Compliance with the Official Languages Policy (Presentation to CSOs)
partnerName: Civil Society Organizations & UNDP Sri Lanka
abstract: Prepared for civil society organizations in December 2022, this presentation details OLP compliance across 30 public institutions in Northern, Eastern, North Western, and Uva provinces. Employing mystery customer audits, checklist verifications, and stakeholder interviews, the study maps actual language barriers. It establishes a monitoring and audit framework to empower local CSOs to advocate for language rights, specifically evaluating the service experiences of Sinhalese-speaking minorities in the North/East and Tamil-speaking minorities in the remaining provinces.

title: Presentation of Mystery Audit: Compliance with the Official Languages Policy (OLP)
abstract: This presentation sets out the findings of 'Mystery Audit' assessments conducted across public institutions to evaluate OLP compliance. It utilizes independent customer auditors to assess receptionist bilingualism, signboard trilinguality, phone help desks, and the general availability of official forms in local languages. *Note: Detailed source passages for this document are not available in the current project context, and this entry is reconstructed provisionally based on administrative references in the language project materials.*

title: Revaluation of the Past and Reconciliation
abstract: This research monograph addresses the complex social and historical narratives that shape post-conflict reconciliation in Sri Lanka. It explores the revaluation of historical events, transitional justice, collective memory, and community healing, proposing strategic peace education and cultural dialogue frameworks to bridge ethnic divides. *Note: Detailed source passages for this document are not available in the current project context, and this entry is reconstructed provisionally based on the project titles list.*
